newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission to propose new tobacco rules, subsidies.
newsitem.headline: Commission to propose new tobacco rules, subsidies.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to propose on Wednesday that the European Union strengthen measures to discourage smoking while keeping and reforming its controversial tobacco subsidy programme.

Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn plans to make a last-ditch effort to convince his colleagues to end tobacco subsidies, but he is outnumbered by those who think that is unrealistic, Commission officials said.

They are expected to propose instead targeting the money at higher-quality tobacco, offering buyouts to entice farmers to abandon tobacco and doubling the one percent levy on subsidies that is used to finance the EU's anti-smoking efforts.

At the same time, the Commission is set to adopt a communication suggesting new measures the EU or national governments could take to regulate tobacco products in areas such as health warnings, nicotine content and additives.

Flynn has been campaigning to phase out the programme that channels almost one billion Ecus a year to tobacco farmers, arguing that it compromises the EU's effort to curtail its 500,000 annual smoking-related deaths.

But Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler argues that would put 135,000 farmers -- plus 65,000 seasonal workers and tobacco processors -- out of work without curbing smoking since consumers would simply buy imported products, officials said.
Tobacco farmers would have a hard time diversifying to other products since they generally work on small patches of land that is not suitable for anything else, they added.

The Commission is expected to propose instead using the subsidies to encourage farmers to switch to higher-quality tobacco, thus attracting a higher market price that could possibly allow the sector to survive eventually without EU help.
Flynn has complained that on average the quality of EU tobacco is so low that its commercial value is only one fifth of the subsidies used to grow it.
The Commission is expected to endorse separate Flynn- sponsored proposals for regulating tobacco consumption, which officials said would rely heavily on recommendations by a group of cancer experts.

That group recommended setting new limits on the nicotine content of cigarettes, banning additives other than tobacco unless proven to be non-toxic and strengthening health warnings on tobacco products.
Flynn has been unsuccessful in his effort to persuade EU ministers to adopt a total ban on tobacco advertising.
